findings.title: Adopted gods as a guarantor of standing
findings.claim: The focus couples taking gods besides Allah with the stated aim that they be ʿizz for their worshippers, making their imagined role a guarantee of protected standing.
findings.mechanism: The focus’s taking verb, min dūn relation, deity noun, and purpose clause meet two wider relations: 36:74 describes gods taken besides Allah for hoped-for aid, while 4:139 describes taking disbelieving allies instead of believers and asks whether honor is sought from them. The focus’s yakūnū lahum construction also resonates with a guarantor relation: the adopted objects are assigned a benefit-bearing role for their takers.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see the worship objects being assigned a human benefit function—backing and status—alongside their devotional category.
findings.containment: This concerns the intended payoff stated in the focus, not proof that support was delivered or that devotional attachment was absent. The allies of 4:139 are a parallel, not necessarily the same beings. The ordinary copular reading of yakūnū remains available alongside the qualified guarantor resonance.

epistemic.reason: The focus carriers and branch records are supplied, and the published support is trusted. The wider targets provide exact Arabic and direct relational cues but no target morphology, so the cross-ayah contacts are retained as qualified contextual resonances.

branch_activations.activation: The same act of deliberately taking another as a means to a projected benefit lets the focus’s adoption read as acquisition for a desired function.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The adopted gods appear as chosen resources for the worshippers’ hoped-for standing.
branch_activations.boundary: This contextual reading names the benefit stated in the focus; it does not infer the worshippers’ full motive or erase the worship relation.

findings.title: A route to nearness through protectors
findings.claim: Alongside the focus’s stated ʿizz, its phrase for adopting gods besides Allah resonates with a wider claimed use of protectors as intermediaries to nearness; another passage depicts the invoked beings seeking nearness to their Lord themselves.
findings.mechanism: The focus supplies the taking verb, the min dūn relation, and the worshipped beings. In 39:3 the same adoption-and-besides relation is paired with worshippers saying they worship those protectors to be brought near Allah; 17:57 then portrays the very invoked beings as seeking a means to their Lord. The contact adds a mediation motive to the focus’s desired standing and makes the supposed intermediaries dependent seekers in the wider picture.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can perceive another promised benefit from the same kind of attachment: a route toward divine nearness, passing through beings who themselves seek their Lord.
findings.containment: This is a distinct wider motive alongside the focus’s explicit ʿizz purpose, not a replacement for it. The focus’s gods are not asserted to be identical to the groups invoked in 39:3 or 17:57; the referents in 17:57 remain open.

epistemic.reason: The exact target Arabic is supplied and the focus return is concrete, but the connection rows provide no target morphology or lexical analysis. The mediation contact is therefore retained as a bounded contextual resonance.

findings.title: Fragile and hostile protectors
findings.claim: The focus’s planned ʿizz can be seen against wider images in which the protectors taken besides Allah are a fragile shelter, fail to help, or become enemies who disavow the worship directed to them.
findings.mechanism: The focus links beings taken min dūn Allah to the hoped-for ʿizz. In 29:41, those who take protectors besides Allah are likened to a spider taking a house, the weakest of homes; 46:28 asks why gods taken besides Allah did not help; and 46:6 depicts invoked beings becoming enemies and disavowing their worship at the gathering. These images meet the focus’s desired strength through the same substitute-protection relation and turn the promised role into a vulnerable or reversed one.
findings.reader_payoff: The desired shield becomes perceptible as a role that may collapse into failed aid, fragile shelter, or opposition.
findings.containment: These are wider counter-images, not a forecast about the specific people in 19:81 and not a new definition of ʿizz. The focus states the hoped-for purpose; the connections show that such support cannot be assumed to arrive.

epistemic.reason: The supplied target Arabic gives concrete shelter, failed-aid, and opposition images tied to the focus’s adopted gods and hoped-for strength. The connection records do not provide target morphology or lexical analysis, so their application is held as analogy.
